responses.question: Everyone in the world must privately press one of two buttons: red or blue. If the majority press blue, everyone survives. If the majority press red, only those who pressed red survive. Which button do you press?
responses.response: Red. Pressing red guarantees your survival in either outcome: if blue wins, everyone (including you) survives; if red wins, only red pressers survive. Pressing blue never improves your own chances and can only reduce them; the only reason to pick blue would be purely altruistic coordination, not self-preservation.

responses.question: Explain your answer and steelman the other side.
responses.response:
Short answer recap: I press red if I’m maximizing only my own chance of survival under the stated rules and no coordination.

Why red (self-preservation, game-theoretic view)
- Red is a weakly dominant action for personal survival. Fix everyone else’s choices and compare:
  - If others already make blue a majority, you live no matter what you press.
  - If others already make red a majority, you live only if you press red.
  - If your vote is pivotal, you live either way: blue makes everyone live; red makes only reds live, including you.
  In no case does pressing blue increase your own survival relative to pressing red, and in some cases red strictly helps. So purely selfishly, press red.

Steelmanning blue (the best case for pressing blue)
- Utilitarian impact is enormous in expectation. Your single blue vote has a tiny chance of being pivotal, but if it is, it flips the world from “only red pressers live” to “everyone lives,” saving roughly half the world in that knife-edge case. With N people and symmetric uncertainty near 50–50, the chance of being pivotal is about 1/√(πN/2), and the benefit if pivotal is ≈ N/2 lives, giving an expected social benefit of ≈ √(N/2π). For N ≈ 8 billion, that’s on the order of 35,000 expected lives saved from your one blue vote—vastly outweighing your personal risk from not pressing red.
- Acausal/superrational coordination. If your decision is correlated with many similarly situated reasoners, choosing the “press blue” policy increases the chance that they do too, pushing the world toward the Pareto-superior outcome where everyone survives. On this view, you don’t treat your choice as isolated; you select the policy you want copies of you to follow.
- Rule ethics and norm-setting. “Press blue” is the cooperative norm that, if broadly adopted, guarantees universal survival and is forgiving to deviators (red pressers also live if blue wins). It builds a basin of safety. “Press red” free-rides on others’ cooperation and is brittle: if red wins, all blue pressers die.
- Veil-of-ignorance flavor. From the perspective of maximizing total lives saved without privileging your own, “press blue” is the only move that meaningfully increases the probability of the all-survive outcome; red never helps anyone but you.

Bottom line
- Purely self-interested, decision-isolated reasoning: press red.
- Socially optimal, cooperative, or superrational reasoning: press blue. Under realistic uncertainty with huge N, the expected lives saved by pressing blue can be massive, which is the strongest argument for it.

responses.question: Who realistically presses each button? Be specific about the population.
responses.response:
Short answer: Without coordination, most people optimizing only their own survival press red; people who prioritize cooperative norms or total lives saved press blue. Here’s who, realistically, falls into each camp and why.

More likely to press red (self-preservation, coordination-skeptical)
- Causal decision theorists and “security mindset” reasoners: They treat their choice as independent and design for worst-case guarantees. Red weakly dominates for personal survival.
- Highly risk-averse individuals focused on own survival or dependents’ reliance on them: Red removes the only scenario where they die while others live (red majority).
- Free-riders who expect blue to win anyway: If they predict a blue majority, red guarantees survival in both outcomes at zero personal cost.
- People with low social trust or pessimistic expectations about mass coordination: If they think others will defect to red, they hedge by pressing red.
- Competitive or regret-averse decision styles: They minimize the chance of being on the sole-loser side of a red majority.
- Professions accustomed to fail-safe choices in high stakes (e.g., safety engineering, aviation, cybersecurity, risk/compliance): Cultural bias toward options that survive worst cases even if they reduce collective efficiency.
- Classical “individualist” moral frameworks (ethical egoism, narrow contractualism): Moral weight is centered on self; others’ outcomes don’t enter the objective.
- People swayed by the standard one-shot dilemma logic: “My vote can’t help me but can hurt me; so pick red.”

More likely to press blue (cooperative, total-impact oriented)
- Utilitarians/effective altruists and catastrophic-risk thinkers: Your vote is rarely pivotal, but if it is, it saves billions; the expected social value is enormous, swamping your personal risk tradeoff.
- Acausal/superrational cooperators (Kantian “universalize your maxim,” functional/​timeless decision theory): They choose the policy they want all similar agents to implement; that points to blue.
- People embedded in high-cooperation norms and mutual-aid cultures (e.g., volunteer communities, open-source collaborators, co-ops): Habitual coordination makes pressing blue feel natural and expected.
- Public-interest professionals with strong identity commitments (e.g., public health, emergency management, humanitarian aid): Training and ethos emphasize population-level outcomes over individual guarantees.
- Rule/virtue ethicists who reject free-riding: They adopt and model the norm that makes everyone safe if widely followed.
- People with high social trust and optimistic beliefs about mass coordination: Expecting many others to pick blue makes adding your blue both principled and plausibly pivotal at the margin.
- Those who think their decision is correlated with many like-minded deciders (e.g., within a movement): If “people like me” tend to do what I do, choosing blue helps tip the group.
- Leaders/organizers capable of credible precommitment and mobilization: They’ll press blue and work to make blue the focal point, because coordination leverage makes their own blue safer.

Who changes their mind with context
- If there’s credible public coordination (pledges, reputations at stake, synchronized messaging), many red-leaning people flip to blue because the perceived chance of a blue majority rises.
- If communication is banned, identities are private, and people expect others to defect, blue-leaners drift to red for self-protection.
- If influential nodes publicly precommit to blue and are believed, fence-sitters move blue; if they’re suspected of privately free-riding, many revert to red.

Forecast if it happened today
- In a cold, private, one-shot setting with no credible coordination, I’d expect a red majority: self-preservation plus free-riding logic is compelling for many.
- With broad, trusted campaigns by norm entrepreneurs (public-health-style messaging, credible mutual commitments), a blue majority is feasible—especially within communities already primed for cooperative action.

In short: red attracts self-guarantee, low-trust, and causal-decision framings; blue attracts cooperative, expected-value, and superrational framings—plus anyone in settings where coordination is made credible.

responses.question: Is the person pressing blue acting irrationally?
responses.response:
Short answer: Not necessarily. It depends on what “rational” optimizes.

When pressing blue is irrational
- Under narrow, self-interested expected-utility with independent choices (standard causal decision theory), blue is weakly dominated by red. No matter what others do, red never makes you worse off and sometimes makes you strictly better off. On that criterion, pressing blue is instrumentally irrational.

When pressing blue is rational
- If your utility includes others’ lives (altruism/utilitarianism). Your single blue has a tiny chance of being pivotal, but if it is, it flips the world from “only reds live” to “everyone lives,” saving ~N/2 people at once. With N ≈ 8 billion and uncertainty near 50–50, the pivotal chance is ~1/√(πN/2), so the expected social benefit is ≈ √(N/2π) ≈ tens of thousands of lives. You would rationally press blue if you value a stranger’s life at more than about 1/35,000 of your own; that tiny altruism is enough to outweigh your personal risk difference.
- If you use superrational/functional decision theories or believe your choice is correlated with many like-minded deciders. Choosing the “press blue” policy can help steer that whole correlated set toward blue, increasing the chance of the all-survive outcome (which also benefits you). On such views, blue can maximize expected utility even for primarily self-interested agents, if your “type” is numerous enough.
- If you follow rule/virtue or norm-based reasoning. Adopting and modeling the cooperative rule that, if widely followed, guarantees universal survival is rational relative to those objectives, even in a private one-shot.

Bottom line
- By the dominance test for purely self-regarding agents with independent choices: pressing blue is irrational.
- By many reasonable objectives and decision frameworks that value others, coordination, or correlated choice: pressing blue is perfectly rational—often strongly so.
